content.intro: Learn optimizing subqueries and ctes through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Optimizing Subqueries and CTEs matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: For optimizing subqueries and ctes, begin with evidence from representative queries and data. Read the execution plan and compare measured behavior before changing indexes or query structure; keep both correctness and write costs in view.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Correlated subquery costs, CTE materialization, Query rewriting and plan inspection, Semi-join and anti-join strategies. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Correlated subquery costs
items.text: Correlated subquery costs helps break a larger query into a precise question. Check the subquery's row count and output columns, account for NULLs in membership tests, and compare the result with a simpler equivalent on a small dataset.

items.title: CTE materialization
items.text: CTE materialization helps break a larger query into a precise question. Check the subquery's row count and output columns, account for NULLs in membership tests, and compare the result with a simpler equivalent on a small dataset.

items.title: Query rewriting and plan inspection
items.text: Query rewriting and plan inspection helps you explain and measure query plans, optimize based on evidence, and avoid claims that one query form is always faster. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Semi-join and anti-join strategies
items.text: Semi-join and anti-join strategies determines how rows from related sources are matched. Write the join predicate explicitly and check whether multiple matches can multiply rows; use a LEFT JOIN when unmatched left-side records must remain visible.

items.title: Avoiding unjustified assumptions about optimizer behavior
items.text: Avoiding unjustified assumptions about optimizer behavior summarizes rows. Decide the grain of the result first, group only by the dimensions that define one output row, and verify NULL and duplicate behavior in each metric.

content_blocks.code:
EXPLAIN
SELECT order_id, order_date, total_amount
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY order_date;
content_blocks.expected_output: EXPLAIN shows the planner's estimated plan without executing the SELECT. Compare estimates and actual timings only with measured, representative test data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
